title: React Routing and Application Structure
subtitle: Organize multi-page experiences inside a React application.
description: Understand client-side routing, navigation, route structure and how to organize larger React applications.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Understand React Routing and Application Structure

Welcome to Lesson 8: React Routing and Application Structure. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “React Routing and Application Structure”. The goal is to organize multi-page experiences inside a React application.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
Routing maps a URL to a view so users can open, refresh, and share meaningful destinations. A route should have a clear path and an explicit fallback for unknown paths.

blocks.question: A route hides private content but the underlying data endpoint permits anyone to fetch it. Is the data protected?
options: Yes, because React rendered it conditionally.
Only if the page is blue.
No; authorization must be enforced at the trusted data/server boundary.
blocks.explanation: UI route guards improve navigation but do not replace server or database authorization.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. UI route guards improve navigation but do not replace server or database authorization.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. UI route guards improve navigation but do not replace server or database authorization.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning
Navigation state is not a replacement for authorization. A protected view must still verify access at the trusted data or server boundary.
